title: Russia Unveils New RVV-SDM Missile to Boost Su-57E Export Push
excerpt: Rosoboronexport launches global campaign for the medium-range air-to-air missile alongside Russia's fifth-generation stealth fighter, with India among the most serious potential buyers.
body:
• Russia's Rosoboronexport began marketing the RVV-SDM medium-range air-to-air missile on July 29, designed primarily for the Su-57E export fighter.
  • The missile features an active/passive radar seeker and claimed electronic-countermeasures resistance, completing a layered weapons package alongside the RVV-MD2 and RVV-BD missiles.
  • India remains the frontrunner buyer after Putin offered unrestricted Su-57 technology access in June 2026, reviving the shelved FGFA partnership eight years after New Delhi walked away.

Russia launched a global marketing campaign for the RVV-SDM, a new medium-range air-to-air missile designed for its Su-57E fifth-generation fighter, state arms exporter Rosoboronexport announced on July 29, 2026. The move, reported by TASS, positions the Su-57E not as a stand-alone airframe but as a complete air-combat ecosystem — a critical distinction as Moscow courts foreign buyers, with India at the top of the list.

The Missile

The RVV-SDM bridges the gap between Russia's short-range RVV-MD2 and long-range RVV-BD, creating what Rosoboronexport describes as a layered air-to-air weapons architecture for short-, medium- and beyond-visual-range engagements. According to Rostec, the missile can engage aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles and unmanned aerial systems in contested electronic-warfare environments, operating day and night at target altitudes from 15 metres to 25 kilometres, against targets moving at up to Mach 3.

Its disclosed guidance system combines inertial navigation, a radio-correction mid-course link and an active/passive radar seeker — a dual-mode terminal sensor that could allow the weapon to home on targets that are jamming or emitting, reducing reliance on active radar emissions in the final phase. Rosoboronexport claims improved range, power-to-weight ratio and jamming resistance over earlier R-77-family missiles, though it has released no numerical maximum range or no-escape-zone data, according to Army Recognition.

"The missile can be used by other Russian-built aircraft after appropriate modification and may also be integrated into the armament systems of foreign-made platforms."

— Rostec announcement via TASS, July 29, 2026

Combat Context

The export push comes as the Su-57's combat role in Ukraine has evolved dramatically. Once designed for stealthy deep-penetration missions, the handful of operational Su-57s — believed to number around nine, according to The War Zone — have been largely confined to standoff strike operations, launching Kh-59 and Kh-69 cruise missiles from well behind the front lines.

Since early 2026, open-source imagery has shown Su-57s carrying external R-73/R-74 and R-77-series missiles — a configuration that trades stealth for firepower. Aviation journalist Thomas Newdick reported in July 2026 that Russia had reconfigured at least some Su-57s to hunt Ukrainian drones and cruise missiles threatening refineries and defence-industrial sites. On July 6, a Su-57 was photographed over Omsk apparently trying, and failing, to prevent Ukrainian strike drones from reaching Russia's largest oil refinery, Defence Blog reported.

Russia has previously claimed unverified air-to-air kills with the Su-57. In October 2022, General Sergey Surovikin stated the fighter had scored kills in both air-to-air and air-to-ground roles; Russian sources subsequently claimed Su-57s shot down Ukrainian Su-27 and Su-24 aircraft using R-37 missiles. No hard evidence has surfaced to corroborate these claims, and independent analysts have not confirmed any Su-57 aerial victories.

The India Angle

For India, the RVV-SDM announcement adds substance to an already tantalising offer. On June 5, President Putin told the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum that Russia would supply Su-57s to India with "completely unrestricted" technology access — source codes, radar architecture, mission software — a dramatic departure from the controlled Su-57E export package.

The offer directly targets the grievances that led India to walk away from the $6 billion FGFA joint-development programme in 2018: limited workshare, restricted technology transfer and concerns over engine maturity and stealth performance. Russia is now dangling the full Su-57 family, including the two-seat Su-57D command variant that first flew in May 2026, and the possibility of licensed production at facilities already building the Su-30MKI.

The Indian Air Force operates at roughly 29 to 31 fighter squadrons against an authorised strength of 42.5. Its indigenous fifth-generation answer, the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft, is unlikely to enter service before the mid-2030s. A Su-57 purchase could serve as a bridge, but New Delhi would need ironclad guarantees on software access, weapons integration authority and upgrade freedom — precisely the issues that torpedoed the FGFA a decade ago, Army Recognition noted.

What's Next

The RVV-SDM campaign marks Russia's clearest signal yet that it wants the Su-57E evaluated as a battle-ready weapons system, not just an airframe. But the decisive test remains whether Moscow can demonstrate credible seeker performance, production capacity and sustained logistical support.

For India and other prospective buyers, the question is whether Russia's export pitch — layered missiles, full technology access, joint production — can survive scrutiny on delivery timelines, sanctions exposure and the Su-57's mixed combat record in Ukraine. With China deploying J-20 stealth fighters near the Indian border and the AMCA still years away, the clock is ticking on New Delhi's fifth-generation decision.
nri_angle: India is the frontrunner buyer for the Su-57E and has been offered unprecedented full technology access by Russia, directly addressing the IAF's critical fighter squadron deficit while the indigenous AMCA remains a decade away.
author: Diaspora Desk
